The first person to hold the office of **prime minister of the Russian Empire** was Count Sergei Yulyevich Witte.  
He was appointed **19 October 1905** (effective 20 October 1905) as Chairman of the Council of Ministers—Russia’s first constitutionally‑established prime‑minister‑like role.  

*Source: Wikipedia – “Sergei Witte” entry, which lists his term as 19 October 1905 – 22 April 1906.*

Count**Sergei Yulyevich Witte** (Russian: Сергей Юльевич Витте, romanized:_Sergey Yulyevich Vitte_, IPA:[[sʲɪrˈɡʲej ˈjʉlʲjɪvʲɪtɕ ˈvʲitːɛ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-1)29 June [O.S. 17 June] 1849–13 March [O.S. 28 February] 1915), also known as **Sergius Witte**, was a Russian statesman who served as the first prime minister of the Russian Empire, replacing the emperor as head of government. Neither liberal nor conservative, he attracted foreign capital to boost Russia's industrialization. Witte's strategy was to avoid the danger of wars.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-2)
Count Witte served under the final two emperors of Russia, Alexander III (r.1881–1894) and Nicholas II (r.1894–1917).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-twilightxiii-3) During the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, he had risen to a position in which he controlled all the traffic passing to the front along the lines of the Odessa Railways. As finance minister from 1892–1903, Witte presided over extensive industrialisation and achieved government monopoly control over an expanded system of railway lines.

Following months of civil unrest and outbreaks of violence in what became known as the 1905 Russian Revolution, Witte framed the October Manifesto and the accompanying government communication to establish constitutional government. However, he was not convinced it would solve Russia's problems with the Tsarist autocracy. On 20 October 1905 Witte was appointed as the first chairman of the Council of Ministers (effectively prime minister). Assisted by his Council, he designed Russia's first constitution. But within a few months Witte fell into disgrace as a reformer because of continuing court opposition to these changes. He resigned  before the First Duma assembled on 10 May [O.S. 27 April] 1906. Witte was fully confident that he had resolved the main problem: providing political stability to the regime,_[citation needed_] but according to him, the "peasant problem" would further determine the character of the Duma's activity.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-4)
He is widely considered to have been one of the key figures in Russian politics at the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-5)Orlando Figes has described Witte as the 'great reforming finance minister of the 1890s',[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig41-6) 'one of Nicholas's most enlightened ministers',[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig8-7) and as the architect of Russia's new parliamentary order in 1905.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig217-8)

## Family and early life
[edit]
Witte's father, Julius Christoph Heinrich Georg Witte, was from a LutheranBaltic German family.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-9) He converted to Russian Orthodoxy upon his marriage with Yekaterina Fadeyeva. His father was made a member of the knighthood in Pskov but moved as a civil servant to Saratov and Tiflis (present-day Tbilisi, Georgia). Sergei was raised on the estate of his mother's parents. His grandfather was Andrei Mikhailovich Fadeyev, a Governor of Saratov and Privy Councillor of the Caucasus, and his grandmother was Princess Helene Dolgoruki. Sergei had two brothers (Alexander and Boris) and two sisters (Olga and Sophia).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-peoples.ru-10)Helena Blavatsky, noted as a mystic, was their first cousin. Witte studied at a Tiflis gymnasium, but he took more interest in music, fencing and riding than in academics. He finished Gymnasium I in Kishinev[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-11) and began studying Physico-Mathematical Sciences at the Novorossiysk University in Odessa in 1866 and graduated at the top of his class in 1870.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-twilightxiv-12) After completing his studies he devoted some time to journalism in close relations with the Slavophiles and Mikhail Katkov.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-EB1911-13)

Title: The Prime Ministers of the Russian Empire
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,9,10,11,12,13
The Russian Empire is the oldest continuously existing constitutional monarchy after the Kingdom of France. The first Russian constitution was granted by Ivan IV the Terrible, of the Rurik dynasty, who issued the so-called Charter of Alexandrovskaya Sloboda in 1564. This charter established limits on royal power, defined the privileges of the nobility and the rights of the Orthodox clergy, and set out the rights of elected representatives from rural communities and towns. Until the 18th century, there was no formal hierarchy among the ministers serving the Tsar; consequently, there were no official "Prime Ministers," though certain individuals functioned as such "de facto", for instance, Simeon Bekbulatovich under Ivan IV, Nikita Romanovich under Ivan V (1576–1580), Boris Godunov under Theodor I (1580–1591), and Vasily Shuisky under Dmitry I. Following the death of Dmitry I, Mikhail Romanov—a grandson of Nikita—ascended the throne in 1613, having married Irina Dimitrovna, the daughter of Dmitry I. Under Mikhail I, his father, Feodor, served as *de facto* Prime Minister until his death in 1633. Mikhail I’s cousin, Ivan Cherkassky, subsequently took on the roles of Minister of the Treasury and Public Administration, effectively acting as Prime Minister. Upon Ivan’s death in 1642, the Tsarist government remained without a clear leader until the death of Mikhail in 1645. At that point, Boris Morozov assumed the role under Tsar Dmitry II (1645–1676), only to be replaced a few years later by Nikita Odoyevsky. A new constitutional charter, the "Dimitrian Code," was approved by the Zemsky Sabor in 1649; it effectively institutionalized serfdom in exchange for tax exemptions for the Boyars. This constitution formalized the office of the General Chancellor of the Crown,a position that, at the time, was accountable solely to the Tsar. Nikita Minim was one of the most prominent figures to hold this post, remaining in office until 1681. Upon the death of Demetrius II, he was succeeded by his son, Theodore II, who reigned until 1682.

Theodore II appointed Vasily Golitsyn as General Chancellor, an appointment later confirmed by Tsarina Sophia I. Sophia ruled until her death in 1704, sharing power with Tsars Ivan VI (who died in 1696) and Peter I. Following Sophia’s death, Peter I appointed a succession of General Chancellors: first Vasily’s cousin, Boris Golitsyn, then Gavril Golovkin, and finally Alexander Menshikov. Upon Peter’s death, the throne passed to his son, Demetrius III, who died suddenly of smallpox in 1727. The throne then went to his son, Peter II, a child, under the regency of Menshikov, and, following Menshikov’s death, under that of Dimitry Golitsyn. Peter II reigned until 1740; in 1731, he approved the "Golitsyn Reform," a new constitution that established the office of Prime Minister, a role requiring the confidence of the Zemsky Sabor, and introduced elections for the Zemsky Sabor based on a property-based franchise (census suffrage). The Duma became the upper house of Parliament. The first two Russian political parties emerged: the Liberals, led by Golitsyn, and the Conservatives, led first by Golovkin, and subsequently by Andrey Osterman and Ivan Dolgorukov. The Liberals secured a majority, and Dimitry Golitsyn became Prime Minister. Dimitry Golitsyn (Liberal) (1731–1742)
Formerly Chancellor-General, he was the primary architect of the new constitution of 1731. He oversaw a series of significant agrarian and military reforms and established an efficient administration, while curbing the excesses of the nobility. In foreign policy, he maintained peaceful relations with Poland and Austria. Upon the death of Peter II, who left no heirs, Golitsyn recognized the succession of Tsarina Elizabeth, daughter of Peter I. However, she deeply opposed the Prime Minister; in 1742, she dismissed him and dissolved the Zemsky Sobor. The subsequent elections resulted in a victory for the Conservatives.
Andrey Osterman (Conservative) (1742–1747)

An able ambassador and competent Minister of Foreign Affairs, a position reporting directly to the sovereign, who appointed and dismissed the minister independently of the Prime Minister, Osterman had served since the reign of Peter I. He was chosen as Prime Minister by Tsarina Elizabeth, who viewed him as the "lesser evil" within the Conservative Party. Following his death, the Conservatives won the elections once again.
Ivan Dolgorukov (Conservative) (1747–1752)
A nephew of Tsarina Catherine (wife of Peter II), Dolgorukov was a Prime Minister loyal to the Crown, which is perhaps the only positive thing that can be said of him. In 1752, shortly before the elections, the Tsarina dismissed him, urging the Conservatives to select someone with a bit more intelligence. While Dolgorukov was a passable administrator, his decisions regarding foreign and economic policy were disastrous. He was also an opponent of the country’s modernization and Westernization, favoring instead an alliance with the reactionary British Commonwealth.
Aleksey Bestuzhev-Ryumin (Conservative) (1752–1763)

A staunch executor of the Tsarina’s will, Bestuzhev strengthened ties with France and Austria, fostered the Westernization of customs by modernizing the tax system, the administration, and the army, improved education, and resolved the crisis between the Orthodox Church and the Crown, which had persisted since 1715. She also had to address the issue of succession, as Elizabeth had no offspring with her husband, the Tsar-Consort Oleksiy Hryhorovych Rozumovsky, also known as Alexis I. There were two main contenders: the Tsarina’s nephew, Karl Dieter Ulrich of Holstein-Gottorp,the legitimate heir, though not particularly well-liked by the court, and the Duke of Courland, Ivan Antonovich Romanov-Brunswick-Lüneburg, a descendant of Ivan VI who held significant influence among the Russian nobility. The marriage of Karl Dieter Ulrich to Sophia of Anhalt bolstered his standing, as Elizabeth developed a very close relationship with her. Ultimately, the parliament and the wishes of Elizabeth I led to the accession of Peter III, who, in a surprising move, officially elevated his wife to the throne as Sophia II. Bestuzhev-Ryumin fell out of favor with the royal couple for opposing this decision in favor of the resurgent Liberal faction; subsequently, when Peter and Sophia dissolved the "Sobor" (parliament) in 1763 and called for new elections, the Conservatives were defeated.
Mikhail Vorontsov (Liberal) (1763–1767)
A personal friend of the Imperial couple, Vorontsov supported the reforms envisioned by Peter, as well as the foreign policy—firmly pro-Austrian, pro-Polish, and pro-French—advocated by the Tsarina. Upon his death in 1767, he was succeeded by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Nikita Panin.
Nikita Panin (Liberal) (1767–1781)

A skilled diplomat, he brought to fruition the ambitious reform agenda of his predecessor (encompassing judicial, administrative, and military reforms). During his long tenure, Tsar Peter III the Magnanimous passed away at the age of only 50. Paul I ascended the throne alongside his mother; the two engaged in a sort of affectionate rivalry, as Paul held conservative views, whereas Sophia II was a liberal reformer. Friction with the young Paul I, combined with deteriorating health, led Panin to resign in 1781—though not before successfully negotiating a marital alliance with Austria, which saw Anna Petrovna wed Joseph II. In his place, Sophia II managed to appoint another liberal: General Yemelyan Pugachev.
Yemelyan Pugachev (Liberal) (1781–1796)
A general from a small-landowner background who had distinguished himself valiantly in the war against Prussia, Pugachev continued the reformist path laid out by his predecessors. Notable achievements during his term included agrarian reform and the expansion of the franchise. Pugachev maintained an excellent working relationship with the Empress, though his rapport with her son was far less harmonious. While the Winter Palace consistently denied rumors of an affair between the Prime Minister and the Empress, the outbreak of revolution within the British Commonwealth fundamentally altered the European balance of power. It was during this period that Russia began establishing relations with the Kingdom of the United American Provinces, a realm ruled by the deposed British House of Stuart. Meanwhile, the revolutionary-led Second British Commonwealth adopted a secular, federal constitution and forged friendly ties with both Russia and the Kingdom of France. However, in 1794, a military coup led by General Arthur Wesley restored the old, confessional, and centralized Commonwealth, suppressing the Irish Catholics and the Scots in a bloodbath. France declared war in defense of the Irish Catholics, and Russia joined the coalition. In 1796, Empress Sophia II died, and the Conservatives, bolstered by the support of the Orthodox Church and Tsar Paul I, prevailed in the elections.
Gavrila Derzhavin (Conservative) (1796–1806)

An esteemed poet and astute politician, Derzhavin managed to maintain the network of alliances established by his predecessor. In domestic policy, he made concessions to the Russian Orthodox Church and the aristocracy; he also sought to promote Russian culture through educational reform, fostered communication by creating a modern Russian postal system, and encouraged the development of the empire’s peripheral regions, including the colonization of Alaska. During his administration, the British Commonwealth was decisively defeated, and Ireland became an independent constitutional monarchy under the French House of Orléans. In 1806, high taxation led to the Conservatives' defeat at the polls. That same year, Tsar Paul I passed away, succumbing to nephritis. His successor, Tsar Alexander I, was a staunch liberal, a fact that also influenced the election outcome.
Mikhail Speransky I (Liberal) (1806–1812)
During his first term, Speransky dedicated himself to an extensive reform of the Russian legal system and reorganized the electoral districts to make them more representative. In foreign policy, I confirm the alliance of the three great European liberal powers—France, under King Louis XVI and Prime Minister Napoleon Bonaparte; the Holy Roman Empire, under Emperor Francis II and Supreme Chancellor Francesco Melzi d'Eril; and Russia itself, against the reactionary powers, the Commonwealth of Great Britain under Lord Protector William Cavendish; the Spanish Empire under King Ferdinand VII and Prime Minister Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo di Calabria; and the Polish-Lithuanian Empire, ruled by Stanisław II of Bourbon-Leszczyński—brother of the King of France and a staunch reactionary—with the support of his powerful Prime Minister, Adam Kazimierz Czartoryski. However, an excessive zeal for modernization alienated the Russian Orthodox Church. In particular, the extension of taxes on agricultural income to include monasteries proved to be an extremely unpopular move, even within his own party. This led to the defeat of Speransky and the Liberals in the 1812 elections.
Nikolay Saltykov (Conservative) (1812–1818)

A general and highly regarded Chief of Staff under Paul I, he was elected Prime Minister by the conservative majority. In foreign policy, he maintained the alliance with the liberal powers; domestically, however, he sought to undo many of his predecessor’s reforms, bringing him into conflict with the Tsar. He proved unable to manage the transition from an agrarian to an industrial economy, which resulted in his failure to be re-elected.
Mikhail Speransky II (Liberal) (1818–1830)
Speransky returned to government with a more moderate agenda, avoiding the mistakes of his first term. He focused on infrastructure and the education system, and implemented a banking reform designed to finance agricultural enterprise. Victorious in the 1824 elections, he oversaw the imperial succession in 1825: following the death of Alexander I, his brother Constantine I ascended to the throne. In 1826, he inaugurated the *Peter I*, the first ironclad warship of the Imperial Russian Navy. Furthermore, the massive colonization of Alyeska began. In 1829, the Zemsky Sabor approved an electoral law that introduced universal male suffrage, as well as suffrage for women based on property or tax-paying qualifications. In 1830, he left politics for health reasons and dedicated himself to writing essays until his death in 1839. He was succeeded by his protégé and Minister of the Interior, Sergei Trubetskoy.
Sergei Trubetskoy (Liberal) (1830–1836)
Having succeeded Speransky in 1830, Trubetskoy attempted to continue along the path of reform; however, in 1831, Constantine I died suddenly without issue and was succeeded by his brother, Nicholas I, a conservative and militarist. Throughout his term, Trubetskoy was constantly obstructed by the Tsar. The only notable achievement of the Trubetskoy administration was the reform of the penal code, which included the abolition of the crime of witchcraft and the removal of the ban preventing non-Christians from holding political office. In 1836, the Conservatives returned to power.
Sergei Uvarov (Conservative) (1836–1842)

Sergey Volkonsky (Liberal) (1860–1872)
Volkonsky initiated the true industrialization of the Russian Empire, overseeing the construction of the massive Trans-Siberian railway network and the installation of telegraph lines. The massive colonization of Russian America led to the discovery of gold in Northern California and a brief war with the United Kingdom of America over control of the region, a conflict won by the Russian Empire. The Hawaiian Islands became a protectorate of the Russian Empire, and in 1863, Russian ships under Commodore Pyotr Anzhu forced the opening of Japanese ports. In 1865, the Imperial family suffered a grievous loss when the Tsarevich Nicholas died following an accident. In 1866, the Liberals were re-elected. During his second term, Volkonsky had to diplomatically counter the rising militarism of Poland by supporting the Holy Roman Empire. He succeeded in negotiating the independence of various Slavic peoples in the Balkans, but this heightened tensions between the Russian Empire and the Ottoman Empire, which subsequently joined the Polish alliance network. Meanwhile, the remilitarization of the Commonwealth of England proceeded at an accelerated pace. In domestic policy, the reform of the bureaucracy fostered the development of a middle class in both urban and rural areas. However, Volkonsky was brought down by a scandal when a deeply entrenched system of corruption—linked to the control of electoral districts—was uncovered. Forced to serve as a scapegoat, he handed over leadership of the party to the Minister of the Interior, Mikhail Loris-Melikov.
Mikhail Loris-Melikov (Liberal) (1872–1884)

Count Loris-Melikov, Prince of Lori, was the first Georgian to be appointed Prime Minister of the Russian Empire. He immediately set to work on reforming the electoral districts to eliminate the scourge of corruption, and under his leadership, all adult women finally gained the right to vote. However, the lax economic policies he adopted exacerbated social inequalities. In 1878, the Social Democratic Party, led by Mikhail Bakunin and Pyotr Kropotkin, and the Agrarian Party, led by Lev Tolstoy, entered parliament. This caused great alarm among the upper-middle class of Russian society, who began to abandon the Liberal Party. A law placing the imperial secret services under the authority of a permanent parliamentary commission was, unfortunately, passed just one day before a failed assassination attempt against the Tsar,an event the opposition was quick to exploit. The final blow to the Liberal era in Russia came with the budget deficit of 1883, which forced the government to introduce a series of taxes that angered both the upper-middle class and the lower classes; the latter held protests that were subsequently suppressed by the police. Alexander II died in 1883 and was succeeded by the conservative Alexander III. In 1884, the Conservatives returned to power.
Konstantin Pobedonostsev (Conservative) (1884–1890)
A personal friend of Tsar Alexander III, Pobedonostsev rose to power following a sweeping victory for the Conservatives in the 1884 elections. He immediately ushered in an intensely reactionary period, seeking to roll back many of the social gains achieved in previous decades. To soften the blow, Pobedonostsev strengthened the social welfare system, introducing pensions and maternity incentives. Yet this welfare-oriented blanket could not prevent the Russian people from noticing the tightening of restrictions on freedom of expression, the violent repression of labor movements, the crackdown on universities, and the extensive concessions granted to the Orthodox Church. Furthermore, in 1889, Pobedonostsev was compelled to implement a very stringent fiscal policy targeting larger fortunes, thereby alienating the sympathies of major industrialists as well as thoseof the middle-class. In 1890, the Conservatives lost their majority.
Lev Tolstoy (Agrarian) (1890–1902)

Writer and political activist Lev Tolstoy came to power with a compromise proposal designed to ease social tensions. An extensive welfare system and agreements with the reformist wing of the Orthodox clergy helped quell a wave of strikes. Following the death of Tsar Alexander III and the accession of his son, Nicholas II, a personal friend of Tolstoy, a period of reconciliation between social classes began. Tolstoy championed some of the first animal welfare policies in the history of the Empire: he banned the culling of stray animals, improved the conditions of shelters, and prohibited cruel or unusual methods of animal slaughter. Concerned about rising pollution, he enacted the first laws to protect rivers and lakes from industrial waste and initiated reforestation efforts. The Tolstoy administration passed legislation to protect minors and encouraged women to enter universities, even facilitating the candidacy and election of women in local government. In foreign policy, Tolstoy pursued a strict pacifism, favoring diplomatic solutions and positioning Russia as a respected arbiter in various international disputes. St. Petersburg hosted the 1900 World’s Fair. However, the protectionist policies implemented by the Agrarian government led to a contraction in trade and an industrial crisis, resulting in an increase in both public debt and taxation. This led to the defeat of the Agrarian Party in 1902 and the return of the Liberals to power.
Sergei Witte I (Liberal) (1902–1908)
Witte worked to reduce public spending and the tax burden, while encouraging private enterprise by cutting back on the country’s bureaucracy. In foreign policy, Witte found himself at odds with the rising military power of Korea, leading to a brief war in 1904 that ended without a clear victor. Witte promoted the modernization of infrastructure and the military; however, the growing popularity of the Social Democrats—fueled by rising social inequality—led to a decline in support for his administration. This resulted in a parliamentary deadlock, which in 1908 forced an alliance between the Liberals and the Conservatives, following the refusal of the Agrarians (led by Grigori Rasputin) to participate. The Liberals, who held the majority, were compelled to yield to the Conservatives' demands and surrender the premiership to Pyotr Stolypin.
Pyotr Stolypin (Conservative) (1908–1911)

The remedy proved worse than the ailment: Stolypin attempted what was effectively a parliamentary coup, seeking to diminish the political power of the working masses in favor of industrial elites. In 1911, a faction within the Liberal Party voted for a motion of no confidence, leading to the formation of a coalition government comprising Liberals, Social Democrats, and Agrarians.
Sergei Witte II (Liberal) (1911–1914)
Witte’s second administration managed, with great difficulty, to restore social cohesion within the country by implementing a series of significant reforms—including the establishment of maximum working hours, a contractual minimum wage, the protection of the right to strike, educational reform, and legal safeguards for small-scale property owners. However, following the death of Witte, the resurgence of Anglo-French hostilities and the looming threat of a violent European war led voters to favor the Agrarian Party.
Grigory Rasputin (Agrarian) (1914–1920)
A student at an Orthodox seminary in his youth, who later earned a degree in philosophy, Rasputin, a man of magnetic personality and undeniable charm, kept Russia out of the conflict and successfully mediated a peace settlement satisfactory to all parties involved. In domestic policy, Rasputin advocated for a cultural revival of Russian traditions; however, his heavy emphasis on the Orthodox faith, combined with the perceived contradiction between his private life, he was a libertine with numerous mistresses and illegitimate children, and the values he championed, led to a collapse in support for the Agrarian Party and the subsequent victory of the Russian Social Democratic Party.
Vladimir Ulyanov (Social Democrat) (1920–1924)

Brother of Alexander Ulyanov, who died in a carriage accident in 1898, Vladimir Ulyanov emerged as the leader of the Social Democratic Party following a fiercely contested congress in 1918, where he defeated the incumbent leader, Alexander Kerensky. He subsequently won the 1920 elections on a platform of "gentle revolution," which included reforms to the civil code and family law (introducing divorce, civil marriage, and the opening of cemeteries to all religious denominations), the implementation of federalism within the Empire, and a policy of international cooperation. This latter effort culminated in 1924 with the founding of the League of Nations, headquartered in Moscow. Unfortunately, a stomach tumor forced him to resign.
Alexander Kerensky (Social Democrat) (1924–1932)

Count**Sergei Yulyevich Witte** (Russian: Сергей Юльевич Витте, romanized:_Sergey Yulyevich Vitte_, IPA:[[sʲɪrˈɡʲej ˈjʉlʲjɪvʲɪtɕ ˈvʲitːɛ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-1)29 June [O.S. 17 June] 1849–13 March [O.S. 28 February] 1915), also known as **Sergius Witte**, was a Russian statesman who served as the first prime minister of the Russian Empire, replacing the emperor as head of government. Neither liberal nor conservative, he attracted foreign capital to boost Russia's industrialization. Witte's strategy was to avoid the danger of wars.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-2)
Count Witte served under the final two emperors of Russia, Alexander III (r.1881–1894) and Nicholas II (r.1894–1917).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-twilightxiii-3) During the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, he had risen to a position in which he controlled all the traffic passing to the front along the lines of the Odessa Railways. As finance minister from 1892–1903, Witte presided over extensive industrialisation and achieved government monopoly control over an expanded system of railway lines.
texts.2:
Following months of civil unrest and outbreaks of violence in what became known as the 1905 Russian Revolution, Witte framed the October Manifesto and the accompanying government communication to establish constitutional government. However, he was not convinced it would solve Russia's problems with the Tsarist autocracy. On 20 October 1905 Witte was appointed as the first chairman of the Council of Ministers (effectively prime minister). Assisted by his Council, he designed Russia's first constitution. But within a few months Witte fell into disgrace as a reformer because of continuing court opposition to these changes. He resigned  before the First Duma assembled on 10 May [O.S. 27 April] 1906. Witte was fully confident that he had resolved the main problem: providing political stability to the regime,_[citation needed_] but according to him, the "peasant problem" would further determine the character of the Duma's activity.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-4)
He is widely considered to have been one of the key figures in Russian politics at the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-5)Orlando Figes has described Witte as the 'great reforming finance minister of the 1890s',[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig41-6) 'one of Nicholas's most enlightened ministers',[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig8-7) and as the architect of Russia's new parliamentary order in 1905.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig217-8)
texts.3:
## Family and early life
[edit]
Witte's father, Julius Christoph Heinrich Georg Witte, was from a LutheranBaltic German family.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-9) He converted to Russian Orthodoxy upon his marriage with Yekaterina Fadeyeva. His father was made a member of the knighthood in Pskov but moved as a civil servant to Saratov and Tiflis (present-day Tbilisi, Georgia). Sergei was raised on the estate of his mother's parents. His grandfather was Andrei Mikhailovich Fadeyev, a Governor of Saratov and Privy Councillor of the Caucasus, and his grandmother was Princess Helene Dolgoruki. Sergei had two brothers (Alexander and Boris) and two sisters (Olga and Sophia).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-peoples.ru-10)Helena Blavatsky, noted as a mystic, was their first cousin. Witte studied at a Tiflis gymnasium, but he took more interest in music, fencing and riding than in academics. He finished Gymnasium I in Kishinev[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-11) and began studying Physico-Mathematical Sciences at the Novorossiysk University in Odessa in 1866 and graduated at the top of his class in 1870.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-twilightxiv-12) After completing his studies he devoted some time to journalism in close relations with the Slavophiles and Mikhail Katkov.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-EB1911-13)

texts.0: The Russian Empire is the oldest continuously existing constitutional monarchy after the Kingdom of France. The first Russian constitution was granted by Ivan IV the Terrible, of the Rurik dynasty, who issued the so-called Charter of Alexandrovskaya Sloboda in 1564. This charter established limits on royal power, defined the privileges of the nobility and the rights of the Orthodox clergy, and set out the rights of elected representatives from rural communities and towns. Until the 18th century, there was no formal hierarchy among the ministers serving the Tsar; consequently, there were no official "Prime Ministers," though certain individuals functioned as such "de facto", for instance, Simeon Bekbulatovich under Ivan IV, Nikita Romanovich under Ivan V (1576–1580), Boris Godunov under Theodor I (1580–1591), and Vasily Shuisky under Dmitry I. Following the death of Dmitry I, Mikhail Romanov—a grandson of Nikita—ascended the throne in 1613, having married Irina Dimitrovna, the daughter of Dmitry I. Under Mikhail I, his father, Feodor, served as *de facto* Prime Minister until his death in 1633. Mikhail I’s cousin, Ivan Cherkassky, subsequently took on the roles of Minister of the Treasury and Public Administration, effectively acting as Prime Minister. Upon Ivan’s death in 1642, the Tsarist government remained without a clear leader until the death of Mikhail in 1645. At that point, Boris Morozov assumed the role under Tsar Dmitry II (1645–1676), only to be replaced a few years later by Nikita Odoyevsky. A new constitutional charter, the "Dimitrian Code," was approved by the Zemsky Sabor in 1649; it effectively institutionalized serfdom in exchange for tax exemptions for the Boyars. This constitution formalized the office of the General Chancellor of the Crown,a position that, at the time, was accountable solely to the Tsar. Nikita Minim was one of the most prominent figures to hold this post, remaining in office until 1681. Upon the death of Demetrius II, he was succeeded by his son, Theodore II, who reigned until 1682.
texts.1:
Theodore II appointed Vasily Golitsyn as General Chancellor, an appointment later confirmed by Tsarina Sophia I. Sophia ruled until her death in 1704, sharing power with Tsars Ivan VI (who died in 1696) and Peter I. Following Sophia’s death, Peter I appointed a succession of General Chancellors: first Vasily’s cousin, Boris Golitsyn, then Gavril Golovkin, and finally Alexander Menshikov. Upon Peter’s death, the throne passed to his son, Demetrius III, who died suddenly of smallpox in 1727. The throne then went to his son, Peter II, a child, under the regency of Menshikov, and, following Menshikov’s death, under that of Dimitry Golitsyn. Peter II reigned until 1740; in 1731, he approved the "Golitsyn Reform," a new constitution that established the office of Prime Minister, a role requiring the confidence of the Zemsky Sabor, and introduced elections for the Zemsky Sabor based on a property-based franchise (census suffrage). The Duma became the upper house of Parliament. The first two Russian political parties emerged: the Liberals, led by Golitsyn, and the Conservatives, led first by Golovkin, and subsequently by Andrey Osterman and Ivan Dolgorukov. The Liberals secured a majority, and Dimitry Golitsyn became Prime Minister. Dimitry Golitsyn (Liberal) (1731–1742)
Formerly Chancellor-General, he was the primary architect of the new constitution of 1731. He oversaw a series of significant agrarian and military reforms and established an efficient administration, while curbing the excesses of the nobility. In foreign policy, he maintained peaceful relations with Poland and Austria. Upon the death of Peter II, who left no heirs, Golitsyn recognized the succession of Tsarina Elizabeth, daughter of Peter I. However, she deeply opposed the Prime Minister; in 1742, she dismissed him and dissolved the Zemsky Sobor. The subsequent elections resulted in a victory for the Conservatives.
Andrey Osterman (Conservative) (1742–1747)
texts.2:
An able ambassador and competent Minister of Foreign Affairs, a position reporting directly to the sovereign, who appointed and dismissed the minister independently of the Prime Minister, Osterman had served since the reign of Peter I. He was chosen as Prime Minister by Tsarina Elizabeth, who viewed him as the "lesser evil" within the Conservative Party. Following his death, the Conservatives won the elections once again.
Ivan Dolgorukov (Conservative) (1747–1752)
A nephew of Tsarina Catherine (wife of Peter II), Dolgorukov was a Prime Minister loyal to the Crown, which is perhaps the only positive thing that can be said of him. In 1752, shortly before the elections, the Tsarina dismissed him, urging the Conservatives to select someone with a bit more intelligence. While Dolgorukov was a passable administrator, his decisions regarding foreign and economic policy were disastrous. He was also an opponent of the country’s modernization and Westernization, favoring instead an alliance with the reactionary British Commonwealth.
Aleksey Bestuzhev-Ryumin (Conservative) (1752–1763)
texts.3:
A staunch executor of the Tsarina’s will, Bestuzhev strengthened ties with France and Austria, fostered the Westernization of customs by modernizing the tax system, the administration, and the army, improved education, and resolved the crisis between the Orthodox Church and the Crown, which had persisted since 1715. She also had to address the issue of succession, as Elizabeth had no offspring with her husband, the Tsar-Consort Oleksiy Hryhorovych Rozumovsky, also known as Alexis I. There were two main contenders: the Tsarina’s nephew, Karl Dieter Ulrich of Holstein-Gottorp,the legitimate heir, though not particularly well-liked by the court, and the Duke of Courland, Ivan Antonovich Romanov-Brunswick-Lüneburg, a descendant of Ivan VI who held significant influence among the Russian nobility. The marriage of Karl Dieter Ulrich to Sophia of Anhalt bolstered his standing, as Elizabeth developed a very close relationship with her. Ultimately, the parliament and the wishes of Elizabeth I led to the accession of Peter III, who, in a surprising move, officially elevated his wife to the throne as Sophia II. Bestuzhev-Ryumin fell out of favor with the royal couple for opposing this decision in favor of the resurgent Liberal faction; subsequently, when Peter and Sophia dissolved the "Sobor" (parliament) in 1763 and called for new elections, the Conservatives were defeated.
Mikhail Vorontsov (Liberal) (1763–1767)
A personal friend of the Imperial couple, Vorontsov supported the reforms envisioned by Peter, as well as the foreign policy—firmly pro-Austrian, pro-Polish, and pro-French—advocated by the Tsarina. Upon his death in 1767, he was succeeded by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Nikita Panin.
Nikita Panin (Liberal) (1767–1781)
texts.4:
A skilled diplomat, he brought to fruition the ambitious reform agenda of his predecessor (encompassing judicial, administrative, and military reforms). During his long tenure, Tsar Peter III the Magnanimous passed away at the age of only 50. Paul I ascended the throne alongside his mother; the two engaged in a sort of affectionate rivalry, as Paul held conservative views, whereas Sophia II was a liberal reformer. Friction with the young Paul I, combined with deteriorating health, led Panin to resign in 1781—though not before successfully negotiating a marital alliance with Austria, which saw Anna Petrovna wed Joseph II. In his place, Sophia II managed to appoint another liberal: General Yemelyan Pugachev.
Yemelyan Pugachev (Liberal) (1781–1796)
A general from a small-landowner background who had distinguished himself valiantly in the war against Prussia, Pugachev continued the reformist path laid out by his predecessors. Notable achievements during his term included agrarian reform and the expansion of the franchise. Pugachev maintained an excellent working relationship with the Empress, though his rapport with her son was far less harmonious. While the Winter Palace consistently denied rumors of an affair between the Prime Minister and the Empress, the outbreak of revolution within the British Commonwealth fundamentally altered the European balance of power. It was during this period that Russia began establishing relations with the Kingdom of the United American Provinces, a realm ruled by the deposed British House of Stuart. Meanwhile, the revolutionary-led Second British Commonwealth adopted a secular, federal constitution and forged friendly ties with both Russia and the Kingdom of France. However, in 1794, a military coup led by General Arthur Wesley restored the old, confessional, and centralized Commonwealth, suppressing the Irish Catholics and the Scots in a bloodbath. France declared war in defense of the Irish Catholics, and Russia joined the coalition. In 1796, Empress Sophia II died, and the Conservatives, bolstered by the support of the Orthodox Church and Tsar Paul I, prevailed in the elections.
Gavrila Derzhavin (Conservative) (1796–1806)
texts.5:
An esteemed poet and astute politician, Derzhavin managed to maintain the network of alliances established by his predecessor. In domestic policy, he made concessions to the Russian Orthodox Church and the aristocracy; he also sought to promote Russian culture through educational reform, fostered communication by creating a modern Russian postal system, and encouraged the development of the empire’s peripheral regions, including the colonization of Alaska. During his administration, the British Commonwealth was decisively defeated, and Ireland became an independent constitutional monarchy under the French House of Orléans. In 1806, high taxation led to the Conservatives' defeat at the polls. That same year, Tsar Paul I passed away, succumbing to nephritis. His successor, Tsar Alexander I, was a staunch liberal, a fact that also influenced the election outcome.
Mikhail Speransky I (Liberal) (1806–1812)
During his first term, Speransky dedicated himself to an extensive reform of the Russian legal system and reorganized the electoral districts to make them more representative. In foreign policy, I confirm the alliance of the three great European liberal powers—France, under King Louis XVI and Prime Minister Napoleon Bonaparte; the Holy Roman Empire, under Emperor Francis II and Supreme Chancellor Francesco Melzi d'Eril; and Russia itself, against the reactionary powers, the Commonwealth of Great Britain under Lord Protector William Cavendish; the Spanish Empire under King Ferdinand VII and Prime Minister Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo di Calabria; and the Polish-Lithuanian Empire, ruled by Stanisław II of Bourbon-Leszczyński—brother of the King of France and a staunch reactionary—with the support of his powerful Prime Minister, Adam Kazimierz Czartoryski. However, an excessive zeal for modernization alienated the Russian Orthodox Church. In particular, the extension of taxes on agricultural income to include monasteries proved to be an extremely unpopular move, even within his own party. This led to the defeat of Speransky and the Liberals in the 1812 elections.
Nikolay Saltykov (Conservative) (1812–1818)
texts.6:
A general and highly regarded Chief of Staff under Paul I, he was elected Prime Minister by the conservative majority. In foreign policy, he maintained the alliance with the liberal powers; domestically, however, he sought to undo many of his predecessor’s reforms, bringing him into conflict with the Tsar. He proved unable to manage the transition from an agrarian to an industrial economy, which resulted in his failure to be re-elected.
Mikhail Speransky II (Liberal) (1818–1830)
Speransky returned to government with a more moderate agenda, avoiding the mistakes of his first term. He focused on infrastructure and the education system, and implemented a banking reform designed to finance agricultural enterprise. Victorious in the 1824 elections, he oversaw the imperial succession in 1825: following the death of Alexander I, his brother Constantine I ascended to the throne. In 1826, he inaugurated the *Peter I*, the first ironclad warship of the Imperial Russian Navy. Furthermore, the massive colonization of Alyeska began. In 1829, the Zemsky Sabor approved an electoral law that introduced universal male suffrage, as well as suffrage for women based on property or tax-paying qualifications. In 1830, he left politics for health reasons and dedicated himself to writing essays until his death in 1839. He was succeeded by his protégé and Minister of the Interior, Sergei Trubetskoy.
Sergei Trubetskoy (Liberal) (1830–1836)
Having succeeded Speransky in 1830, Trubetskoy attempted to continue along the path of reform; however, in 1831, Constantine I died suddenly without issue and was succeeded by his brother, Nicholas I, a conservative and militarist. Throughout his term, Trubetskoy was constantly obstructed by the Tsar. The only notable achievement of the Trubetskoy administration was the reform of the penal code, which included the abolition of the crime of witchcraft and the removal of the ban preventing non-Christians from holding political office. In 1836, the Conservatives returned to power.
Sergei Uvarov (Conservative) (1836–1842)
texts.9:
Sergey Volkonsky (Liberal) (1860–1872)
Volkonsky initiated the true industrialization of the Russian Empire, overseeing the construction of the massive Trans-Siberian railway network and the installation of telegraph lines. The massive colonization of Russian America led to the discovery of gold in Northern California and a brief war with the United Kingdom of America over control of the region, a conflict won by the Russian Empire. The Hawaiian Islands became a protectorate of the Russian Empire, and in 1863, Russian ships under Commodore Pyotr Anzhu forced the opening of Japanese ports. In 1865, the Imperial family suffered a grievous loss when the Tsarevich Nicholas died following an accident. In 1866, the Liberals were re-elected. During his second term, Volkonsky had to diplomatically counter the rising militarism of Poland by supporting the Holy Roman Empire. He succeeded in negotiating the independence of various Slavic peoples in the Balkans, but this heightened tensions between the Russian Empire and the Ottoman Empire, which subsequently joined the Polish alliance network. Meanwhile, the remilitarization of the Commonwealth of England proceeded at an accelerated pace. In domestic policy, the reform of the bureaucracy fostered the development of a middle class in both urban and rural areas. However, Volkonsky was brought down by a scandal when a deeply entrenched system of corruption—linked to the control of electoral districts—was uncovered. Forced to serve as a scapegoat, he handed over leadership of the party to the Minister of the Interior, Mikhail Loris-Melikov.
Mikhail Loris-Melikov (Liberal) (1872–1884)
texts.10:
Count Loris-Melikov, Prince of Lori, was the first Georgian to be appointed Prime Minister of the Russian Empire. He immediately set to work on reforming the electoral districts to eliminate the scourge of corruption, and under his leadership, all adult women finally gained the right to vote. However, the lax economic policies he adopted exacerbated social inequalities. In 1878, the Social Democratic Party, led by Mikhail Bakunin and Pyotr Kropotkin, and the Agrarian Party, led by Lev Tolstoy, entered parliament. This caused great alarm among the upper-middle class of Russian society, who began to abandon the Liberal Party. A law placing the imperial secret services under the authority of a permanent parliamentary commission was, unfortunately, passed just one day before a failed assassination attempt against the Tsar,an event the opposition was quick to exploit. The final blow to the Liberal era in Russia came with the budget deficit of 1883, which forced the government to introduce a series of taxes that angered both the upper-middle class and the lower classes; the latter held protests that were subsequently suppressed by the police. Alexander II died in 1883 and was succeeded by the conservative Alexander III. In 1884, the Conservatives returned to power.
Konstantin Pobedonostsev (Conservative) (1884–1890)
A personal friend of Tsar Alexander III, Pobedonostsev rose to power following a sweeping victory for the Conservatives in the 1884 elections. He immediately ushered in an intensely reactionary period, seeking to roll back many of the social gains achieved in previous decades. To soften the blow, Pobedonostsev strengthened the social welfare system, introducing pensions and maternity incentives. Yet this welfare-oriented blanket could not prevent the Russian people from noticing the tightening of restrictions on freedom of expression, the violent repression of labor movements, the crackdown on universities, and the extensive concessions granted to the Orthodox Church. Furthermore, in 1889, Pobedonostsev was compelled to implement a very stringent fiscal policy targeting larger fortunes, thereby alienating the sympathies of major industrialists as well as thoseof the middle-class. In 1890, the Conservatives lost their majority.
Lev Tolstoy (Agrarian) (1890–1902)
texts.11:
Writer and political activist Lev Tolstoy came to power with a compromise proposal designed to ease social tensions. An extensive welfare system and agreements with the reformist wing of the Orthodox clergy helped quell a wave of strikes. Following the death of Tsar Alexander III and the accession of his son, Nicholas II, a personal friend of Tolstoy, a period of reconciliation between social classes began. Tolstoy championed some of the first animal welfare policies in the history of the Empire: he banned the culling of stray animals, improved the conditions of shelters, and prohibited cruel or unusual methods of animal slaughter. Concerned about rising pollution, he enacted the first laws to protect rivers and lakes from industrial waste and initiated reforestation efforts. The Tolstoy administration passed legislation to protect minors and encouraged women to enter universities, even facilitating the candidacy and election of women in local government. In foreign policy, Tolstoy pursued a strict pacifism, favoring diplomatic solutions and positioning Russia as a respected arbiter in various international disputes. St. Petersburg hosted the 1900 World’s Fair. However, the protectionist policies implemented by the Agrarian government led to a contraction in trade and an industrial crisis, resulting in an increase in both public debt and taxation. This led to the defeat of the Agrarian Party in 1902 and the return of the Liberals to power.
Sergei Witte I (Liberal) (1902–1908)
Witte worked to reduce public spending and the tax burden, while encouraging private enterprise by cutting back on the country’s bureaucracy. In foreign policy, Witte found himself at odds with the rising military power of Korea, leading to a brief war in 1904 that ended without a clear victor. Witte promoted the modernization of infrastructure and the military; however, the growing popularity of the Social Democrats—fueled by rising social inequality—led to a decline in support for his administration. This resulted in a parliamentary deadlock, which in 1908 forced an alliance between the Liberals and the Conservatives, following the refusal of the Agrarians (led by Grigori Rasputin) to participate. The Liberals, who held the majority, were compelled to yield to the Conservatives' demands and surrender the premiership to Pyotr Stolypin.
Pyotr Stolypin (Conservative) (1908–1911)
texts.12:
The remedy proved worse than the ailment: Stolypin attempted what was effectively a parliamentary coup, seeking to diminish the political power of the working masses in favor of industrial elites. In 1911, a faction within the Liberal Party voted for a motion of no confidence, leading to the formation of a coalition government comprising Liberals, Social Democrats, and Agrarians.
Sergei Witte II (Liberal) (1911–1914)
Witte’s second administration managed, with great difficulty, to restore social cohesion within the country by implementing a series of significant reforms—including the establishment of maximum working hours, a contractual minimum wage, the protection of the right to strike, educational reform, and legal safeguards for small-scale property owners. However, following the death of Witte, the resurgence of Anglo-French hostilities and the looming threat of a violent European war led voters to favor the Agrarian Party.
Grigory Rasputin (Agrarian) (1914–1920)
A student at an Orthodox seminary in his youth, who later earned a degree in philosophy, Rasputin, a man of magnetic personality and undeniable charm, kept Russia out of the conflict and successfully mediated a peace settlement satisfactory to all parties involved. In domestic policy, Rasputin advocated for a cultural revival of Russian traditions; however, his heavy emphasis on the Orthodox faith, combined with the perceived contradiction between his private life, he was a libertine with numerous mistresses and illegitimate children, and the values he championed, led to a collapse in support for the Agrarian Party and the subsequent victory of the Russian Social Democratic Party.
Vladimir Ulyanov (Social Democrat) (1920–1924)
texts.13:
Brother of Alexander Ulyanov, who died in a carriage accident in 1898, Vladimir Ulyanov emerged as the leader of the Social Democratic Party following a fiercely contested congress in 1918, where he defeated the incumbent leader, Alexander Kerensky. He subsequently won the 1920 elections on a platform of "gentle revolution," which included reforms to the civil code and family law (introducing divorce, civil marriage, and the opening of cemeteries to all religious denominations), the implementation of federalism within the Empire, and a policy of international cooperation. This latter effort culminated in 1924 with the founding of the League of Nations, headquartered in Moscow. Unfortunately, a stomach tumor forced him to resign.
Alexander Kerensky (Social Democrat) (1924–1932)

He is widely considered to have been one of the key figures in Russian politics at the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-5)Orlando Figes has described Witte as the 'great reforming finance minister of the 1890s',[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig41-6) 'one of Nicholas's most enlightened ministers',[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig8-7) and as the architect of Russia's new parliamentary order in 1905.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig217-8)

## Family and early life
[edit]
Witte's father, Julius Christoph Heinrich Georg Witte, was from a LutheranBaltic German family.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-9) He converted to Russian Orthodoxy upon his marriage with Yekaterina Fadeyeva. His father was made a member of the knighthood in Pskov but moved as a civil servant to Saratov and Tiflis (present-day Tbilisi, Georgia). Sergei was raised on the estate of his mother's parents. His grandfather was Andrei Mikhailovich Fadeyev, a Governor of Saratov and Privy Councillor of the Caucasus, and his grandmother was Princess Helene Dolgoruki. Sergei had two brothers (Alexander and Boris) and two sisters (Olga and Sophia).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-peoples.ru-10)Helena Blavatsky, noted as a mystic, was their first cousin. Witte studied at a Tiflis gymnasium, but he took more interest in music, fencing and riding than in academics. He finished Gymnasium I in Kishinev[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-11) and began studying Physico-Mathematical Sciences at the Novorossiysk University in Odessa in 1866 and graduated at the top of his class in 1870.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-twilightxiv-12) After completing his studies he devoted some time to journalism in close relations with the Slavophiles and Mikhail Katkov.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-EB1911-13)

## Family and early life
### 1905 Revolution and Chairman of the Council of Ministers
[edit]
Prince Alexey D. Obolensky
Witte described the regime's usual "incompetence and obstinacy" in response to the crisis of 1904–1905 as a "mixture of cowardice, blindness and stupidity".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-32)
On 8 January 1905, Witte and Sviatopolk-Mirsky had been approached by a delegation of intellectuals led by Maxim Gorky, who begged them to negotiate with demonstrators. After the government's postings of warnings of 'resolute measures' against street gatherings led by Father Gapon, they worried about violent confrontation, which did take place. They were unsuccessful as the government had believed they could control Fr. Gapon.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-33) Leaving his visiting cards with Witte and Mirsky, Gorky was arrested, along with the other members of the deputations.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-34)
In late 1905, Witte was approached by the tsar's advisers, in an effort to save the country from complete collapse, and on 9 October 1905, he went to the Winter Palace for a meeting. Here he told the tsar 'with brutal frankness' that the country was on the verge of a catastrophic revolution, which he said 'would sweep away a thousand years of history'. He presented the tsar with two choices: either appoint a military dictator, or agree to broad and major reforms. In a memorandum arguing for a manifesto, Witte outlined the reforms needed to appease the masses.
Witte by Ilya Repin in 1903

## Family and early life
### 1905 Revolution and Chairman of the Council of Ministers
He argued for the following reforms: creation of a legislative parliament (Imperial Duma) elected via a democratic franchise; granting of civil liberties; establishing a cabinet government and a 'constitutional order'.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig191-35) Those demands, which basically comprised the political programme of the Liberation Movement, were an attempt to isolate the political Left by pacifying the liberals.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig191-35) Witte emphasised that repression would be only a temporary solution to the problem and a risky one because he believed that the armed forces, whose loyalty was now in question, could collapse if they were to be used against the masses.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig191-35) Most of the military advisers to the tsar agreed with Witte, as did the Governor of Saint Petersburg, Dmitri Feodorovich Trepov, who wielded considerable influence at court. Only when Nicholas II's cousin Grand Duke Nicholas threatened to shoot himself if he did not agree to Witte's demands, following the tsar's request for him to accept appointment as dictator, would the tsar agree. He was embarrassed to have been forced by a former "railway clerk", a man who was a bureaucrat and "businessman," to relinquish his autocratic rule.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig191-35)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-37) Witte later said that the tsar's court were ready to use the Manifesto as a temporary concession, and later return to autocracy "when the revolutionary tide subsided".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig192-36)

## Family and early life
### 1905 Revolution and Chairman of the Council of Ministers
In October Witte was charged with the task of assembling the nation's first cabinet government, and he offered the liberals several portfolios: Ministry of Agriculture to Ivan Shipov; Ministry of Trade and Industry to Alexander Guchkov; Ministry of Justice to Anatoly Koni and the Ministry of Education to Evgenii Troubetzkoy. Pavel Milyukov and Prince Georgy Lvov were also offered ministerial posts. None of those liberals agreed to join the government, though. Witte had to form his cabinet from 'tsarist bureaucrats and appointees lacking public confidence'. The Kadets doubted that Witte could deliver on the promises made by the tsar in October, knowing the tsar's staunch opposition to reform.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-38)
Witte argued that the Tsarist regime could be saved from a revolution only by the transformation of Russia into a 'modern industrial society', in which 'personal and public initiatives' were encouraged by a rechtsstaat that guaranteed civil liberties.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig41-6)
In the two weeks following the October Manifesto, several pogroms took place against Jews, especially in St. Petersburg and Odessa. Witte ordered an official investigation, where it was revealed that the police in the former city had organised, armed and given vodka to, the anti-Semitic crowds, and even participated in the attacks. Witte demanded the prosecution of the chief of police in St. Petersburg, who was involved in the printing of anti-Semitic pamphlets, but the tsar intervened and protected him.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-39) Witte believed that anti-Semitism was 'considered fashionable' among the elite.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-40) In the aftermath of the Kishinev pogrom in 1903, Witte had said that if Jews 'comprise about fifty percent of the membership in the revolutionary parties', it was 'the fault of our government. The Jews are too oppressed'.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-41)

## Family and early life
### 1905 Revolution and Chairman of the Council of Ministers
Milyukov once confronted Witte to ask why he would not commit himself to a constitution. Witte replied that he could not 'because the Tsar does not wish it'.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig195-42) Witte was worried that the court was only using him, as had emerged in talks with members of the Kadet Party.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig195-42)
After his skillful diplomacy Witte was appointed as Chairman of the new Council of Ministers, the equivalent of Prime Minister, and formed [Sergei Witte's Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte's_Cabinet "Sergei Witte's Cabinet"), not belonging to any party, as there were none. No longer was the tsar the head of the government. "Immediately upon my nomination as President of the Imperial Council I made it clear that the Procurator of the Most Holy SynodKonstantin Pobedonostsev, could not remain in office, for he definitely represented the past."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-43) He was replaced by Prince Alexey D. Obolensky. Trepov and Alexander Bulygin were dismissed and, after many discussions, Pyotr Nikolayevich Durnovo was appointed as Minister of Interior on 1 January 1906; his appointment is considered one of the greatest errors Witte made during his administration.

## **Key Facts And Information**
### **Let’s find out more about Sergei Witte!**
Count Sergei Yulyevich Witte was a prominent Russian statesman at the turn of the 20th century, remembered for his role in modernising Russia’s economy and shaping its early constitutional framework. Serving under Tsars Alexander III and Nicholas II, Witte was neither thoroughly liberal nor conservative. Instead, he focused on strengthening Russia through industrial growth, foreign investment, and avoiding unnecessary wars. Witte began his career in the railway industry, where his efficiency and innovative methods brought him to national attention. As Finance Minister from 1892 to 1903, he expanded state control over railways, encouraged heavy industry, and oversaw rapid industrialisation.
![Image 8: Sergei Witte in the early 1880s](blob:http://localhost/f51e6db39cdde27b5ff830f1ae9f6b7d)
Sergei Witte in the early 1880s
*   Witte’s reforms transformed Russia into a more modern economic power, earning him the reputation as the ‘great reforming finance minister’ of the 1890s.  
*   The political upheavals of 1905, known as the Russian Revolution of 1905, pushed Witte into a new role. He helped draft the October Manifesto, which promised a constitution and a national assembly (the Duma). He oversaw the development of Russia’s inaugural constitution in his capacity as the country’s first Prime Minister. However, his departure in 1906, prior to the inaugural Duma, was necessitated by internal opposition within the royal court and concerns regarding the manifesto’s efficacy.

## **Key Facts And Information**
### **Early Life and Career of Sergei Witte**
*   Born into a noble family on 29 June 1849 with Baltic German roots, Sergei Witte was well-educated, graduating at the top of his class in physics and mathematics at the Novorossiysk University in Odessa. Initially intending to become a professor, he was persuaded to join the railways as he developed a strong interest in practical applications of science, particularly in engineering and transport, where his talent for organisation quickly became clear.His career survived setbacks, including a train accident for which he was briefly imprisoned.  
*   Witte was briefly imprisoned in 1875 after a railway accident, the Tiligul disaster, wherein a train carrying army recruits derailed on the Odessa line due to a missing section of track, killing about 100 men. As a senior railway official, despite not being directly at fault, he was held accountable and sentenced to four months in prison.  
*   Nevertheless, he did not serve the full sentence as he was instrumental in coordinating the rail transportation of soldiers and supplies during the Russo-Turkish War (1877–78). Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich was impressed by his efficiency and leadership, and he intervened to reduce the sentence to a mere two weeks. Witte’s reputation was promptly restored, and he resumed his railway duties.  
*   Witte met his future wife in St Petersburg after getting a new job in 1879. A year later, he moved to Kyiv. In 1883, he looked into the costs of railways. He also wrote about the monarchy and social issues in this work, which got the attention of the government.  
*   In 1886, Witte was in charge of the private Southwestern Railways in Kyiv, and under his leadership, the railway became more profitable and efficient. At that time, Witte encountered Tsar Alexander III and advised the tsar’s counsellors that using two large locomotives to transport the imperial train at high speeds was risky, which led to a conflict. In 1888, his predictions were realised with the royal train accident at Borki. Following this incident, Witte secured the position of Director of State Railways.  

## **Key Facts And Information**
### **Early Life and Career of Sergei Witte**
*   By 1889, Witte was appointed Russian Director of Railway Affairs in the Finance Ministry. In this role, he expanded the network, brought most railways under state control, and introduced a merit-based hiring system to replace nepotism. Believing that economic progress depended on education, he promoted technical training for workers and engineers.  
*   Sergei Witte was one of the most important statesmen of late Imperial Russia, best known for his role in modernising the empire’s economy, transport and industry. His career reflected the tensions between reform and autocracy in the final decades of the Romanov dynasty. Furthermore, he proposed customs barriers to protect Russian businesses from international competition, which is similar to economist Friedrich List’s proposals. This signifies that his measures helped to accelerate industrialisation in the late 19th century.

## **Key Facts And Information**
### **Political Career**
*   In 1892, Tsar Alexander III appointed Witte Minister of Finance, a post he held for over a decade. During his tenure, he:  
    *   Expanded the Trans-Siberian Railway to connect European Russia with the Far East.  
    *   Founded technical and commercial schools to train a modern workforce.  
    *   Negotiated favourable trade agreements, including a treaty with Germany in 1894.  
    *   Introduced a state monopoly on alcohol in 1895, boosting government revenue.  
    *   The rouble was put on the gold standard in 1896, attracting foreign investment.  
    *   Introduced labour laws limiting working hours and reformed taxation.

*   Witte’s economic reforms nearly doubled state revenue. However, his marriage to Matilda Ivanovna, a divorcee and converted Jew, caused scandal and damaged his standing among the conservative nobility – although the Tsar continued to support him.  
*   Witte supported the peaceful expansion of trade in East Asia, but his misinterpretation of Japan’s growing power fuelled hostility.  
*   Russia’s acquisition of the Liaodong Peninsula and fortification of Port Arthur enraged Tokyo, resulting in the Russo-Japanese War (1904–1905). Despite the former’s defeat, Witte negotiated the Treaty of Portsmouth in 1905, which limited territorial losses. His diplomatic skills won him the title of Count.  
*   Following military loss and domestic turmoil, including the Bloody Sunday massacre, Witte urged Tsar Nicholas II to make considerable political concessions. He warned that the country was on the verge of a revolution that would overthrow the monarchy. His ideas led to the October Manifesto, which pushed for civil rights and the founding of the Duma, an elected parliament.
![Image 9: A painting by Ilya Repin entitled The Demonstration 17 October 1905.](blob:http://localhost/cc41543c20cc2ae69bc76685cd69cbe4)
A painting by Ilya Repin entitled The Demonstration 17 October 1905.

## **Key Facts And Information**
### **Political Career**
*   The October Manifesto was a document issued by Tsar Nicholas II on 30 October 1905 during the 1905 Russian Revolution. The Tsar agreed to grant some civil rights and allow an elected parliament called the Duma. From then on, laws could not be passed without the Duma’s approval. Although Nicholas was reluctant, the manifesto marked the first step towards a constitution in Russia, which was established in 1906.  
*   Witte was then appointed the first Chairman of Russia's Council of Ministers (Prime Minister). This resulted in a temporary transfer of authority from the tsar. However, his government faced three significant problems:  
    *   Lack of liberal support – many reformers distrusted him and doubted the tsar’s sincerity.  
    *   Continued unrest – strikes, peasant revolts and pogroms continued.  
    *   Court opposition – reactionary advisers worked to undermine his influence.

## **Key Facts And Information**
### **Resignation and Legacy**
*   By April 1906, Witte realised the tsar had no intention of fully honouring the October Manifesto. Disillusioned, he resigned. His final years saw him removed from politics. However, he remained convinced that Russia’s survival hinged on becoming a modern industrial state with protected human liberties.  
*   Witte’s legacy is complex as he modernised Russia’s economy and infrastructure; however, he worked within an autocracy that resisted lasting political reform. His achievements laid the groundwork for industrial growth; however, the failure to match economic progress with democratic change left the empire vulnerable to the revolutionary upheavals that would soon follow.  
*   After his resignation as Russia’s first Prime Minister in 1906, Witte never again held an active role in government administration. Although he remained a member of the State Council, the highest advisory body to the tsar, he had lost the confidence of Nicholas II. The political establishment increasingly sidelined him. Many in the ruling elite saw him as a dangerous reformer who had weakened the autocracy from within, rather than a loyal servant of the tsar. Reactionary forces also targeted Witte. In January 1907, a bomb was discovered in his home, and the investigation revealed that the _Okhrana_, the tsar’s secret police, had been involved, suggesting deliberate intimidation.  
*   After leaving office, Witte spent much of his time abroad, particularly in Biarritz, France, where he began writing his memoirs. However, he returned to St Petersburg in 1908 and continued to give political advice when consulted. During the July Crisis of 1914, on the eve of the First World War, Witte and Grigori Rasputin both urged the Tsar to avoid entering the conflict, warning that it would bring disaster to Russia and Europe. Their advice was ignored, and Russia soon found itself at war.  

## **Key Facts And Information**
### **Resignation and Legacy**
*   Witte died suddenly in February 1915 at his home in St Petersburg, possibly from meningitis or a brain tumour. His funeral, held at the Alexander Nevsky Lavra, was modest for a man of his former standing. His black granite tombstone bears the date 17 October 1905, the day he presented the October Manifesto to the Tsar. He had no biological children but adopted the children of his wife’s first marriage. He had hoped that his title of Count would pass to his grandson, Lev Kyrillovich Naryshkin, but the tsar refused.  
*   Witte’s reputation in the West improved after the posthumous publication of his memoirs in 1921, which had been completed in 1912 but locked away in a French bank until after the deaths of Witte and his contemporaries. The original manuscript is currently housed at Columbia University in the United States. His legacy has received increasing attention in recent years, with the Sergei Witte University in Moscow established in his honour in 1997. Throughout his career, he won various accolades that recognised his diplomatic and economic achievements. They included:  
    *   Russian Orders such as the Order of St. Alexander Nevsky (1906), the Order of the White Eagle (1904), and the Order of St. Vladimir (1913).  
    *   Foreign decorations from countries including France (Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour), Germany (Grand Cross of the Red Eagle), Austria-Hungary (Order of Leopold), Japan, Persia, and many others, demonstrating his international influence.

## **Key Facts And Information**
### Frequently Asked Questions About Sergei Witte
*   Who was Sergei Witte?   
Sergei Witte (1849–1915) was a Russian statesman, minister of Finance (1892–1903), and later Prime Minister (1905–1906). He played a key role in modernising Russia’s economy.

*   What were Witte’s main economic policies?   
He promoted rapid industrialisation through state intervention, foreign investment, protective tariffs, and expansion of heavy industry (coal, steel, and railways).

*   Why did Witte resign in 1906?   
Nicholas II distrusted him, conservatives opposed his reforms, and revolutionaries thought his changes were insufficient. Isolated politically, he resigned as Prime Minister.

Sergei had two brothers (Alexander and Boris) and two sisters (Olga and Sophia).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-peoples.ru-10)Helena Blavatsky, noted as a mystic, was their first cousin. Witte studied at a Tiflis gymnasium, but he took more interest in music, fencing and riding than in academics. He finished Gymnasium I in Kishinev[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-11) and began studying Physico-Mathematical Sciences at the Novorossiysk University in Odessa in 1866 and graduated at the top of his class in 1870.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-twilightxiv-12) After completing his studies he devoted some time to journalism in close relations with the Slavophiles and Mikhail Katkov.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-EB1911-13)

Witte described the regime's usual "incompetence and obstinacy" in response to the crisis of 1904–1905 as a "mixture of cowardice, blindness and stupidity".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-32)
On 8 January 1905, Witte and Sviatopolk-Mirsky had been approached by a delegation of intellectuals led by Maxim Gorky, who begged them to negotiate with demonstrators. After the government's postings of warnings of 'resolute measures' against street gatherings led by Father Gapon, they worried about violent confrontation, which did take place. They were unsuccessful as the government had believed they could control Fr. Gapon.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-33) Leaving his visiting cards with Witte and Mirsky, Gorky was arrested, along with the other members of the deputations.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-34)
In late 1905, Witte was approached by the tsar's advisers, in an effort to save the country from complete collapse, and on 9 October 1905, he went to the Winter Palace for a meeting. Here he told the tsar 'with brutal frankness' that the country was on the verge of a catastrophic revolution, which he said 'would sweep away a thousand years of history'. He presented the tsar with two choices: either appoint a military dictator, or agree to broad and major reforms. In a memorandum arguing for a manifesto, Witte outlined the reforms needed to appease the masses.

He argued for the following reforms: creation of a legislative parliament (Imperial Duma) elected via a democratic franchise; granting of civil liberties; establishing a cabinet government and a 'constitutional order'.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig191-35) Those demands, which basically comprised the political programme of the Liberation Movement, were an attempt to isolate the political Left by pacifying the liberals.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig191-35) Witte emphasised that repression would be only a temporary solution to the problem and a risky one because he believed that the armed forces, whose loyalty was now in question, could collapse if they were to be used against the masses.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig191-35) Most of the military advisers to the tsar agreed with Witte, as did the Governor of Saint Petersburg, Dmitri Feodorovich Trepov, who wielded considerable influence at court. Only when Nicholas II's cousin Grand Duke Nicholas threatened to shoot himself if he did not agree to Witte's demands, following the tsar's request for him to accept appointment as dictator, would the tsar agree. He was embarrassed to have been forced by a former "railway clerk", a man who was a bureaucrat and "businessman," to relinquish his autocratic rule.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig191-35)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-37) Witte later said that the tsar's court were ready to use the Manifesto as a temporary concession, and later return to autocracy "when the revolutionary tide subsided".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig192-36)

In October Witte was charged with the task of assembling the nation's first cabinet government, and he offered the liberals several portfolios: Ministry of Agriculture to Ivan Shipov; Ministry of Trade and Industry to Alexander Guchkov; Ministry of Justice to Anatoly Koni and the Ministry of Education to Evgenii Troubetzkoy. Witte argued that the Tsarist regime could be saved from a revolution only by the transformation of Russia into a 'modern industrial society', in which 'personal and public initiatives' were encouraged by a rechtsstaat that guaranteed civil liberties.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Witte#cite_note-fig41-6)
In the two weeks following the October Manifesto, several pogroms took place against Jews, especially in St. Petersburg and Odessa. Witte ordered an official investigation, where it was revealed that the police in the former city had organised, armed and given vodka to, the anti-Semitic crowds, and even participated in the attacks.
